title: The five remembrances again
hook: five lines for anyone, householder or monk: aging, sickness, death, parting, and heir to my deeds (AN 5.57)
tomorrow: a mother searches for one mustard seed. what does she find?

segments.voice: Yesterday, even the body stays: what walks on is what a person did, and a hadith next door said the same of deeds. Even the body. Today, five lines to hold it all.
screen: `EVEN THE BODY.` → `FIVE LINES TO HOLD IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Some people keep a short list on the lock screen: three goals, a verse, a reminder to drink water. The Buddha gave a list to recite often, and he said it was for everyone: a woman or a man, a householder or someone who has left home. Five lines. They come back today, because this week has been walking right through them.
screen: `A LIST ON THE LOCK SCREEN.` → `FOR EVERYONE, HOME OR MONASTERY.` → `FIVE LINES.`

segments.voice: Here they are, from the Anguttara Nikaya, in plain words. I will grow old; I can't escape aging. I can get sick; I can't escape illness. I will die; I can't escape death. Everyone and everything dear to me will change, and I'll be parted from them. And the fifth: my deeds are my own. I'm the heir to my deeds; whatever I do, good or bad, I'll inherit it. The Buddha gives each line a reason. The first three loosen pride in youth, health and life. The fourth loosens grabbing at what we love. The fifth turns a person toward what they do. Now look back at the week inside them. The weaver's daughter: no one knows when. Nagarjuna's bubble in the wind: fragile. Food and medicine: few supports. The third root: only the practice. The burning house: it stays behind. And the body: even the body. Every one of those is folded into the five. The first four name what can't be held. The last names what's left in your hands: heir to my deeds.
screen: `AGING, ILLNESS, DEATH.` · `PARTED FROM ALL THAT'S DEAR.` · `THE FIFTH: MY DEEDS ARE MY OWN.` · `A WEEK FOLDED INTO FIVE.` · then, large: `HEIR TO MY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Say the five aloud, slowly, once: I will grow old; I can get sick; I will die; I'll be parted from all that's dear; I'm the heir to my deeds. Then sit with whichever line stayed with you, and let the others rest.
The five remembrances: aging, illness, death, parting, and heir to my deeds. Five lines the Buddha said anyone should recall often.
The line to keep: heir to my deeds, the one thing still in your hands. Two weeks of remembering, closed with five lines.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities in several traditions recite the five remembrances in daily chanting, in Pali or in translation; Theravada monasteries and some Zen and Plum Village communities include them in their regular services.

AN 5.57 paraphrased; the reasons for each line are simplified (the sutta speaks of intoxication with youth, health and life; desire and lust for what is dear; and misconduct of body, speech and mind for the fifth). Confirm.
The title says 'again': the five remembrances appear earlier on this path; the voice says only that they 'come back today'.

The practice recites a paraphrase of a real text (AN 5.57); it is not a new prayer.
